text: If some point, which is not the center of the circle, is taken on the diameter of a circle, and some straight-lines radiate from the point towards the (circumference of the) circle, (then) the greatest (straight-line) will be that on which the center (lies), and the least the remainder (of the same diameter). And for the others, a (straight-line) nearer$^\dag$ to the (straight-line) through the center is always greater than a (straight-line) further away. And only two equal (straight-lines) will radiate from the point towards the (circumference of the) circle, (one) on each (side) of the least (straight-line). Let $ABCD$ be a circle, and let $AD$ be its diameter, and let some point $F$, which is not the center of the circle, be taken on $AD$. Let $E$ be the center of the circle. And let some straight-lines, $FB$, $FC$, and $FG$, radiate from $F$ towards (the circumference of) circle $ABCD$. I say that $FA$ is the greatest (straight-line), $FD$ the least, and of the others, $FB$ (is) greater than $FC$, and $FC$ than $FG$.
For let $BE$, $CE$, and $GE$ be joined.
And since for every triangle (any) two sides are greater than the remaining (side) [Prop.~1.20], $EB$ and $EF$ is thus greater than $BF$.
assertion: EB and EF is greater than BF

spans.label: assumption
spans.text: for every triangle (any) two sides are greater than the remaining (side)

text: And $AE$ (is) equal to $BE$ [thus, $BE$ and $EF$ is equal to $AF$].
assertion: BE and EF is equal to AF

text: Thus, $AF$ (is) greater than $BF$.
Again, since $BE$ is equal to $CE$, and $FE$ (is) common, the two (straight-lines) $BE$, $EF$ are equal to the two (straight-lines) $CE$, $EF$ (respectively).
assertion: the two straight-lines BE, EF are equal to CE, EF respectively

spans.label: assertion
spans.text: the two (straight-lines) $BE$, $EF$ are equal to the two (straight-lines) $CE$, $EF$ (respectively)

text: But, angle $BEF$ (is) also greater than angle $CEF$.$^\ddag$
assertion: angle BEF is greater than angle CEF

text: Thus, the base $BF$ is greater than the base $CF$.

spans.label: assertion
spans.text: the base $BF$ is greater than the base $CF$

text: Thus, the base $BF$ is greater than the base $CF$ [Prop.~1.24].

spans.label: assertion
spans.text: the base $BF$ is greater than the base $CF$

text: So, for the same (reasons), $CF$ is also greater than $FG$.
Again, since $GF$ and $FE$ are greater than $EG$ [Prop.~1.20], and $EG$ (is) equal to $ED$, $GF$ and $FE$ are thus greater than $ED$.
assertion: GF and FE are greater than ED

text: Let $EF$ be taken from both.
assertion: EF is subtracted from both sides

text: Thus, the remainder $GF$ is greater than the remainder $FD$.

spans.label: assertion
spans.text: the remainder $GF$ is greater than the remainder $FD$

text: Thus, $FA$ (is) the greatest (straight-line),
$FD$ the least,
and $FB$ (is) greater than $FC$,
and $FC$ than $FG$.
I also say that from point $F$ only two equal (straight-lines) will radiate towards (the circumference of) circle $ABCD$, (one) on each (side) of the least (straight-line) $FD$.
For let the (angle) $FEH$, equal to angle $GEF$, be constructed on the straight-line $EF$, at the point $E$ on it [Prop.~1.23], and let $FH$ be joined.
Therefore, since $GE$ is equal to $EH$, and $EF$ (is) common, the two (straight-lines) $GE$, $EF$ are equal to the two (straight-lines) $HE$, $EF$ (respectively).
assertion: the two straight-lines GE, EF are equal to HE, EF respectively

spans.label: assertion
spans.text: the two (straight-lines) $GE$, $EF$ are equal to the two (straight-lines) $HE$, $EF$ (respectively)

text: And angle $GEF$ (is) equal to angle $HEF$.
Thus, the base $FG$ is equal to the base $FH$ [Prop.~1.4].

spans.label: assertion
spans.text: the base $FG$ is equal to the base $FH$

text: So I say that another (straight-line) equal to $FG$ will not radiate towards (the circumference of) the circle from point $F$.
For, if possible, let $FK$ (so) radiate.
assertion: FK radiates from F equal to FG

frame.supposition: another (straight-line) equal to $FG$ will radiate towards (the circumference of) the circle from point $F$

text: And since $FK$ is equal to $FG$, but $FH$ [is equal] to $FG$, $FK$ is thus also equal to $FH$,
the nearer to the (straight-line) through the center equal to the further away.
assertion: the nearer straight-line equals the further away

spans.label: assertion
spans.text: the nearer to the (straight-line) through the center equal to the further away

text: The very thing (is) impossible.
Thus, another (straight-line) equal to $GF$ will not radiate from the point $F$ towards (the circumference of) the circle.
assertion: no second straight-line equal to GF radiates from F

frame.closes: another (straight-line) equal to $FG$ will radiate towards (the circumference of) the circle from point $F$

spans.label: assertion
spans.text: another (straight-line) equal to $GF$ will not radiate from the point $F$ towards (the circumference of) the circle

text: Thus, (there is) only one (such straight-line).
assertion: only one equal straight-line radiates from F

text: Thus, if some point, which is not the center of the circle, is taken on the diameter of a circle, and some straight-lines radiate from the point towards the (circumference of the) circle, (then) the greatest (straight-line) will be that on which the center (lies), and the least the remainder (of the same diameter). And for the others, a (straight-line) nearer to the (straight-line) through the center is always greater than a (straight-line) further away. And only two equal (straight-lines) will radiate from the same point towards the (circumference of the) circle, (one) on each (side) of the least (straight-line). (Which is) the very thing it was required to show.
